1hx480fw6z: Management ports (SSH, RDP, WinRM) do not need to be open permanently. **Just-in-time** (JIT) access enforces **“deny all inbound traffic”** rules on them in the network security group (NSG) and in Azure Firewall. When a user requests access, Defender for Cloud checks their **RBAC permissions** on the machine; if the request is approved, it temporarily adds an allow rule for the requested source address and duration, then **restores** the previous state. Already established connections are not interrupted, but new ones are blocked after expiration. If rules already exist on the chosen ports, they take priority over the new deny rules. On AWS, JIT removes the relevant rules from the EC2 security groups and creates a new one for temporary access; GCP is not supported.

16giv52adat: For complete protection, Defender for Containers combines four elements. The **Defender sensor** is a lightweight DaemonSet on each node that collects runtime telemetry (Kubernetes events, processes, network) with **eBPF** technology; on AKS it is deployed as a security profile built into the AKS resource provider, elsewhere as an Azure Arc extension. **Azure Policy for Kubernetes** is a pod based on **Gatekeeper v3** that registers as an admission control webhook and makes it possible to enforce configuration rules at scale. **Agentless discovery** gives visibility into clusters, their configuration and their deployments through APIs. Finally, the **registry integration** (ACR, ECR, GAR, GCR) provides image scanning (module 9). Kubernetes audit logs are collected natively on AKS, by an agentless collector on GKE.
1tcu06cpzww: On **AKS**, everything goes through the Azure infrastructure; on **EKS, GKE and any Kubernetes**, clusters must be connected through **Azure Arc** and the components are Arc extensions (`microsoft.azuredefender.kubernetes` for the sensor, `Microsoft.PolicyInsights` for the policy). For agentless discovery on AKS, Defender creates an identity that receives the built-in **Kubernetes Agentless Operator** role on the subscription, with read and **AKS trusted access** rights, then binds a read `ClusterRole` in the data plane. On GKE, a `mdc-containers-k8s-operator` service account receives a custom role that includes `container.clusters.update`: a write permission to know before approving the integration.

The sensor must reach `*.cloud.defender.microsoft.com` on port 443; the `*.ods.opinsights.azure.com` and `*.oms.opinsights.azure.com` domains are no longer required. For a cluster with restricted egress, you must allow the domain names described in the AKS documentation; proxies and private connectivity are supported. The sensor's resource limits are not configurable (about 360 m of CPU and 296 Mi of memory for the node collector pod). 1xqabxe4h4y: Scanning on upload examines blob objects at the time they are uploaded. It handles up to **50 GB per minute per account**; if the rate exceeds this threshold in a sustained way, some objects may not be scanned. For cost predictability, a **monthly cap** of scanned GB can be set per account or for the whole subscription; by default it is **10,000 GB** per account per month, with a possible deviation of 20 GB. When the cap is reached, scanning **stops** for the rest of the month: new objects remain unscanned and **no event** is emitted. The counter resets at midnight UTC at the end of the month, and a change to the cap takes about an hour. Two alerts warn: “75% of cap reached” and “cap reached, scanning stopped.”
11dkejto4z7: **On-demand** scanning (blobs, with Azure Files in preview) launches a one-off scan, for example during an incident. The portal first displays a **cost estimate** based on capacity; there is **no monthly cap** and the cost follows actual usage. Filters (a blob, a container) limit the scope and the cost. It suits incident response and scheduled compliance scans.
1d011ikj4kc: The documentation lists cases: **fragmented** data (uploaded in pieces; a header fragment may be judged corrupt, a tail fragment may look benign), **client-side encrypted** data (the service cannot decrypt it; scan before encrypting, or use Azure-managed encryption at rest) and **backups** (which contain content fragments: false alerts possible). An absence of alerts is therefore never evidence of harmlessness. Ancillary costs are added: storage reads, blob indexing (tags) and Event Grid notifications, and a slight effect on IOPS that you reduce by disabling index tags.
23ettfe04o7: Four paths: **blob index tags** (access control decisions), **security alerts** (SOC), **Event Grid events** (near real-time response) and **Log Analytics** (history for audit). Choose according to the consumer: an access control reads the tags, the SOC reads the alerts, automation reads Event Grid, audit reads Log Analytics.
